title: 4' Bench (no back)
summary: A backless 4-foot bench with a slatted seat, built from 2x4 lumber on a simple open-leg frame.

materials.item: 2x4 dimensional lumber — western red cedar, Douglas fir, or pressure-treated pine
materials.notes: Cedar: naturally weather/rot resistant with a nice red tone, easy to work, needs no sealant (it weathers to gray); costs more — ask for 'knotty' (STK) grade, much cheaper than clear grade. Douglas fir: moderately rot resistant, strong and easy to work, cheaper than cedar, but won't last as long — a good choice if you plan to paint. Pressure-treated: rot resistant and the cheapest option, but lumber quality is often poor and inconsistent, needs 1–4 months of air-drying before painting, and isn't recommended where food is grown. Order 5–10% more than the cut list to allow for variable lumber quality and incorrect cuts.

tools: 10" or 12" miter saw (or appropriate hand saw)
Impact driver for self-driving exterior wood screws
Drill with 1/8" bit for pre-drilling holes

steps.title: Mark, label and cut the lumber
steps.text:
Mark, label and cut lumber in order of B-1 to B-7 into the lengths in the cut list.

Check each piece of lumber for imperfections such as cracks, warping or uneven milling, and discard those portions of lumber.
imageAlts: Isometric diagram of the 4' bench cut pieces B-1 through B-6 with their lengths labeled, from a 48" top board down to 8.5" blocks.
tips: Label each piece of lumber as you measure and cut it.
Keep a separate pile of lumber for each part, B-1 to B-7.
Lightly sanding the cut edges removes splinters and helps with assembly.
Building more than one bench? A stop block on your miter saw keeps every piece the same length.

steps.title: Build the two end frames
steps.text: Place two B-5 pieces on a flat surface. Place two B-4 pieces on either side of the B-5 pieces, aligning the edges as shown. Repeat to build a second, matching frame.
imageAlts: Diagram showing two B-4 and two B-5 boards assembled into a square end frame.
tips: Use a carpenter's square to check each corner forms a right angle — if it's far off, re-check your board lengths.
Building a 90-degree jig can help with assembly of this and the next step.

steps.title: Add the seat slats to each end frame
steps.text:
Place one B-3 piece and four B-6 pieces on top of the frame, as shown, leaving a 1.5" gap between the two B-6 pieces (use a spare 2x4 on end as a spacer).

Use the pre-drilling guide at the end of the packet to pre-drill your screw holes, then secure the lumber into the B-5 and B-4 pieces with an impact driver and 30 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws.

Repeat on the other leg.
imageAlts: Diagram of B-6 and B-3 boards being screwed onto the top of the end frame, with a 1.5" spacer gap called out.

steps.title: Connect the two end frames
steps.text:
Place one B-2 piece in the slot at the base of the two frames created in step 3.

Secure the B-2 lumber on both the left and right sides into the B-5 pieces with an impact driver and 4 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws.
imageAlts: Diagram of a B-2 board connecting the two end frames at the base, with a 90-degree angle called out at the corner.
tips: Check the side stays at 90 degrees using a carpenter's square.

steps.title: Add the seat top
steps.text:
Place two B-1 pieces on top of the frame created in step 4, aligning all edges.

Pre-drill holes for screws, and secure the B-1 lumber with an impact driver and 12 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws.
imageAlts: Diagram of the first two B-1 top boards being screwed onto the bench frame.
tips: Keeping the side at 90 degrees and all edges aligned will help keep the bench square.

steps.title: Finish the seat top and sand
steps.text:
Align three more B-1 middle pieces with equal gaps between the two end boards just installed.

Pre-drill holes for screws, and secure the B-1 lumber with an impact driver and 12 2.5" self-driving exterior wood screws.

Lightly sand the rough edges of the 4' bench.
imageAlts: Diagram of the remaining B-1 top boards being spaced equally and screwed down across the bench frame.

steps.title: Pre-drilling hole guide (template)
steps.text:
Cut out the pre-drilling hole guide along the dotted lines. When drilling, align the edge of the template with the outside edge of the lumber before pre-drilling.

Not all holes are used — not all patterns use the template. Use the assembly steps above for your hole guide. Keep all holes about a thumb's width from the edge (about 1"), even holes that don't use this template.
imageAlts: A printable pre-drilling hole guide template with five marked hole positions and cut lines, plus a close-up showing hole spacing from the board edge.

finishing: Exterior wood treatment can prolong the life of your park elements, but it isn't necessary — these pieces are built to be low-cost, durable and easy to build by design, so it may be more practical to just let the next generation rebuild them when the time comes. If you do want to stain, paint or seal the wood, see the finish resources below.
safety: These are DIY recommendations only — tailor the material, assembly and construction to your own project and site.
Building this assumes some working knowledge of hand and power tools, hardware, fasteners, lumber and basic assembly technique.
Before using any power equipment, review and follow the manufacturer's safety requirements, and don't let anyone use power tools who hasn't done the same.
You (the owner) are responsible for any building and safety codes, permits and regulatory approvals this needs.
Clear the site of trash, hazards and unwanted structures first, and identify any utilities that could interfere before you dig.
Everyone helping build should sign a volunteer waiver.
